worksheet.title: Give Bit the Steps
worksheet.subtitle: Write the arrows to reach the star
worksheet.learning_goal: I can write the arrow steps that get Bit to the star.

parts.title: You make the plan
parts.text: Now YOU give Bit the steps. Look at where Bit is and where the star is. Draw one arrow for each box Bit must move. ➡ goes right, ⬅ goes left.

parts.title: Watch Bit — box 1 to the star on box 3
parts.note: Bit must move 2 boxes right. The steps are ➡ ➡.

parts.title: Box 1 to the star on box 4
parts.prompt: Bit is on box 1. The star is on box 4. Draw the arrows Bit needs (one per box).

parts.title: Box 2 to the star on box 3
parts.prompt: Bit is on box 2. The star is on box 3. Draw the arrows Bit needs.

parts.title: You try — go left
parts.prompt: Bit is on box 4. The star is on box 2. Draw the arrows Bit needs (this time the star is to the left).

parts.title: Big idea
parts.text: When you write the steps that solve a problem, you have made an algorithm. That is exactly what coders do!

teacher_guide.title: Give Bit the Steps
teacher_guide.subtitle: Quick facilitation notes & answer key
teacher_guide.footer_topic: 7. Give Bit the Steps — Teacher Guide

parts.title: What this worksheet teaches
parts.text: Children draw a short set of arrows that moves Bit to the star — choosing the direction and how many steps. Writing the steps that solve a problem is making a simple plan (an algorithm). No coding experience needed.

parts.title: Before you start (no computer needed)
parts.text: No computer — paper and a pencil or crayon. You read each prompt aloud. Optional: tape a row of numbered boxes (and a star) on the floor so a child can walk the steps.

parts.title: How to lead it (about 15 minutes)
text: 1. Show them (you do). Box 1 to the star on box 3: two right arrows.
2. Do one together. Exercise 1 — box 1 to box 4 needs three right arrows.
3. Let them try. Children do Exercise 2 (one right) and Exercise 3 (two left — the star is to the left).

parts.title: Answer key (these are the verified correct answers)
text: Exercise 1 — box 1 → box 4: three right arrows. Exercise 2 — box 2 → box 3: one right arrow.
Exercise 3 — box 4 → box 2: two left arrows.

parts.title: If children get stuck — and ways to adjust
text: Watch for: right number of steps but wrong direction. Check which way the star is first.
Make it easier: count the boxes between Bit and the star, then draw that many arrows.
Make it harder: ask for a plan from box 1 to box 5 (four right arrows).
Make it active: a child walks their drawn arrows on the floor boxes to test the plan.

parts.title: Ontario Kindergarten link (official wording)
text: Problem Solving and Innovating — children create a sequence of directions to reach a goal.
In plain terms: writing the steps that solve a problem — making a simple plan.
No reading is needed from the child — you read each prompt aloud; the child answers by circling, numbering, or drawing arrows.

parts.title: You'll know it worked when
parts.text: The child draws arrows in the right direction and the right number to reach the star.
